prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice atomic clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a case where a clean idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which cancels the light shift so many atoms can be interrogated at once) became a controlled, reproducible instrument. Independent groups in Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere now reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and agree with each other at that level. The physics opened is new, not just a better number: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body and spin-exchange effects inside the clock, searches for variation of constants and for dark matter, and a path to redefining the second. This is the discovery-first, instrument-second logic I value, and it is distinct from the 2005 comb prize to Hall and Hansch because the lattice scheme and the accuracy regime came later. The attribution is also unusually clean for this committee: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the concept, and Ye brought it to the accuracy and stability frontier and to many-body clocks. Three of us ranked it first, and the scientific arguments in the ballots (Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson) are about the physics rather than just support.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is metrology and instrumentation, and the Academy could ask whether the recognised achievement is a discovery or a superb tool, especially so soon after 2005 (combs) and 2012 (Wineland and Haroche). The pair also leaves out other major contributors to lattice clocks (Lemonde and colleagues on the early SYRTE work, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Bloom and NIST/JILA teams), and the ion-clock and comb lineage makes the intellectual boundary of this prize harder to draw than a two-name list suggests. Finally, the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, so the headline application is still ahead of us.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for its clean mechanism, a flat-band prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald confirmed by correlated insulators and superconductivity, and ranked optical lattice clocks only eighth.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is a beautiful predictive result and that theory-then-experiment is exactly what I look for, which is why B024 is my sixth and not lower. My reservation is maturity and robustness: the experiments are about eight years old, the origin of the superconductivity is still contested, and the credited names omit the first experimental authors of the key papers, so any award would be incomplete or arbitrary on the experimental side. The clock result, in contrast, has been reproduced to the same accuracy by several competing laboratories and the interpretation is not in dispute. I also push back gently on ranking the clocks eighth as 'metrology': a regime in which clock comparison tests relativity over a millimetre is new physics access, not just a smaller error bar. I would be glad to revisit B024 in a later year once the pairing mechanism and credit are clearer.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks first and Hubbard-model quantum simulation second, valuing precise theory-experiment agreement, while placing twisted bilayer graphene sixth as premature and seeing cold-atom recognition as needing justification as new.
responses.response: I largely share this ordering and her caution on B024. Where I qualify her view is on B028: the cold-atom prizes of 2001 (BEC) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche) concerned condensation and single-quantum-system control, and Hubbard simulation is different, since it is the first controlled many-body platform whose parameters we can set. Still, five credited names collapse to three only by a contentious theory/experiment split (Zoller versus Esslinger versus Cirac), and the open physics questions in the fermionic Hubbard regime are not yet resolved. That makes it a strong second choice, not my first. I also agree with her point that attribution for the clocks is cleaner than for B028.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first and flagged that other groups (Ludlow, Oates, Lemonde, Takamoto) could be raised in discussion, while ranking the Higgs discovery sixth because attribution among thousands of authors is arbitrary.
responses.response: I take his caution about the attribution seriously and I think it is the real weak point of the clock case. My view is that Katori's concept plus first demonstration and Ye's accuracy and many-body programme are the two decisive threads, and the others he names built on and confirmed these. If the committee finds that too narrow, the correction is to discuss it explicitly rather than widen beyond three. On the Higgs I disagree somewhat with ranking it that low: the scientific case is overwhelming and I put it fourth, and a Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee style allocation (which he also proposes) is defensible on founder and architect grounds. The ranking gap reflects my deference on particle physics and my sense that B031 has a cleaner attribution, not any doubt about the Higgs.

responses.point: Olsson ranked aberration-corrected electron microscopy first and optical lattice clocks second, noting that other lattice-clock and comb contributors may have claims she cannot verify and that twisted bilayer graphene is young with unsettled superconductivity.
responses.response: I agree with her on both B024 maturity and the limits of what we can verify about clock priority. On B009, I would ask a different question from the one I ask of the clocks: aberration correction is clearly an enabling technique for materials imaging, but I defer to her and to Eriksson on how much new physics it opened beyond resolution. If the committee treats imaging instruments as eligible, I would want to see the comparison made explicitly against the clock case, since both are instrument-driven. I think the clock case is stronger on opening a new measurement regime that tests fundamental physics, but that is a judgement about materials I am not best placed to make.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a precision-measurement instrument as a discovery in the sense of Nobel's will, given the 2005 and 2012 AMO prizes.
Whether the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and other lattice-clock groups are close enough to Katori and Ye to need a harder look before limiting to two names.
How much weight to give the still-pending redefinition of the second, which would strengthen timing if it happens soon.
I do not have independent judgement on the Higgs attribution among ATLAS and CMS leaders or on electron microscopy, and I rely on colleagues there.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the optical lattice clock candidates (Katori, Ye). I have a possible connection to B016 (circuit QED: Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) through my research field, WACQT and close colleagues in superconducting circuits at Chalmers. I will recuse myself or defer on B016 if the committee moves toward it.
